title: Supreme Court rejects Verizon bid for $47 million refund of FCC fine
gist: The Supreme Court denied Verizon's bid for a $47M refund of an FCC fine for selling customer location data without consent, ending Verizon's recourse, while AT&T and T-Mobile continue challenging similar fines on the theory that device-location data is not protected under Section 222.

insights.claim: AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon were fined a total of $196 million in 2024 for selling mobile users' real-time location data to aggregators without customer consent, and the Supreme Court has now foreclosed Verizon's path to a $47M refund.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Confirms carriers bear the location-data fines; a precedent on FCC penalty enforcement relevant to telecom regulatory risk.
insights.locator: AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon were fined

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 (Thomas dissenting) that the FCC penalty process does not violate the Seventh Amendment because carriers could have obtained jury trials by refusing to pay and awaiting government collection.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Upholds the FCC's administrative-penalty mechanism, preserving regulators' enforcement leverage over carriers.
insights.locator: The court ruled that the FCC penalty process

insights.claim: AT&T and T-Mobile continue arguing device-location data is not protected under Section 222 (claiming only call-location data is covered), with AT&T remanded to the 5th Circuit and T-Mobile/Sprint seeking Supreme Court review.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A carrier win could gut the FCC's authority to penalize device-location-data sales—watch the 5th Circuit and cert decisions.
insights.locator: Carriers still argue data sales were legal

insights.claim: No new location-data penalties are likely under the current administration, as FCC Chairman Brendan Carr argued against the fines in 2024, agreeing only call-location information is protected.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Signals a materially lighter FCC enforcement posture on carrier data practices under Carr—reduced regulatory risk for telecoms.
